A **process** is a running instance of a program, with its own memory and resources. A **thread** is a sequence of instructions executing inside a process. Every process has at least one thread and can have several.

The main difference is **what they share**:

- Separate processes normally have separate memory. They need explicit ways to exchange data.
- Threads in the same process share memory, but each keeps its own call stack and current execution position. Sharing makes communication easy, but threads can interfere with each other if they change the same data without coordination.

For example, a text editor could use one thread to handle typing and another to check spelling, both accessing the same document inside one process.

Both processes and threads can run concurrently, and on multiple CPU cores they can run at the same time.

# Git internals (synthetic fixture)

Goal: explain what Git stores and predict what everyday commands change.

## Course mode

Style: `tutorial`. About 30 minutes per session.

## Unit 1: Objects

- `git.blob`: file contents as blobs
- `git.tree`: a tree lists names and blobs
- `git.commit-snapshot`: a commit points at one tree and its parents
- `git.hash`: object names are hashes of content

## Unit 2: Branches and HEAD

- `git.branch-pointer`: a branch is a name that points at one commit
- `git.head`: HEAD names the current branch or commit
- `git.fast-forward`: when a merge only moves a pointer
- `git.merge-commit`: a commit with two parents
- `git.detached-head`: HEAD pointing at a commit directly

## Unit 3: Remotes

- `git.remote-tracking`: remote-tracking branches
- `git.fetch-vs-pull`: what each command changes

## Delivery update — 2026-11-12, session 7

Sam: "go with the questions for this course". Question-led tutoring supersedes the historical tutorial/reading-first delivery choice above. Target: 4/5 per subskill, followed by a mixed unit assessment. Preserve short plain-language messages and labelled commit diagrams. Historical completion records do not establish levels.

# Unit 2 tutor notes — prepared 2026-11-12

Private preparation, not learner evidence. Session 7 stopped during diagnosis. Ask the pending merge question before giving any explanation. Use one question per turn. Do not restart the whole diagnostic.

Sources: [checkout](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-checkout), [merge](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-merge). Scope: clean worktree and index, successful commands, ordinary local branches, no hooks or unusual configuration. State these assumptions explicitly. Commit names C1 etc. are symbolic labels; arrows point to parents. Explain command syntax before practical exercises.

## Placement and prerequisites

Existing diagnostic: branch definition; checkout main at C3 to feature at C2; fast-forward condition and action; merge-parent distinction. The last question is unanswered. Accurate definitions alone place at 2; correct independent application can place at 4; partial recognition at 1; no idea at 0. Do not mechanically apply these criteria when an answer supports less. Detached HEAD remains unplaced until checked.

Prerequisites: commit snapshots and parent relationships. Old labels are history, not demonstrated prerequisites. Re-test these later, without silently assigning levels.

For each concept, level 3 means predicting the stated operation with help; level 4 means predicting and explaining independently on a new graph; level 5 adds the listed edge case and a clear teachable explanation.

## Branch as a pointer

New material if needed: a branch name refers to a commit. Committing while attached advances that branch.

Display `C2 -> C1; main=C2; feature=C2; HEAD=feature` before asking for a prediction after a new commit C3. Answer: feature=C3, main=C2, C3's parent=C2. Why question: why can two names refer to the same history? Answer: references can share their target. Flawed claim: making feature duplicates C1 and C2. Answer: it creates another reference, not copies of those commits. Narrower question: which existing commit does the new name initially identify?

Fallback after repeated failed attempts: names are references; a new commit advances the checked-out branch only. Re-test with main checked out and feature unchanged. Edge case: deleting a branch does not necessarily delete its commits; another reference may still reach them. Ask the learner to explain this using two names at the same tip. Do not introduce garbage collection until needed.

## HEAD

New material after diagnosis: HEAD usually refers to the current branch. Switching branches changes HEAD and updates the index and working tree to the destination; it does not move the old branch.

Display `C3 -> C2 -> C1; main=C3; feature=C2; HEAD=main`, clean index/worktree. Prediction: switch to feature. Checked answer: HEAD=feature, both branch tips unchanged, files/index reflect C2. Flawed claim: main must move to C2 because files changed. Narrower question: are the current files and the stored main reference the same thing? Connection: can a snapshot stay stored while another snapshot is displayed? Answer: yes.

Fallback after repeated failed attempts: distinguish stored names from selected snapshot; state the changes above briefly. Re-test: starting on feature, make C4 and then switch to main; feature=C4 while main=C3. Edge case: with uncommitted changes, checkout may preserve nonconflicting changes or refuse an overwriting switch; do not claim every checkout discards local changes.

## Fast-forward

New material after diagnosis: ancestry means following parent links. Fast-forward advances the current branch to a descendant without creating a merge commit.

Display `C3 -> C2 -> C1; main=C1; feature=C3; HEAD=main`. Prediction: successful fast-forward of feature into main. Answer: main=C3, feature=C3, no new commit. Why: C3 already includes C1 in its ancestry. Contrast a graph with main=C4, C4 parent=C1, feature=C3: neither tip is ancestor of the other, so no fast-forward. Narrower question for 'always move to the newer commit': can you reach C4 by following parents from C3?

Fallback: ancestry, not timestamps, determines whether moving the pointer retains both histories. Re-test on C5->C4->C2 with main=C2 and feature=C5. Edge case: `--no-ff` requests a merge commit even when fast-forward is possible; explain the option before asking whether capability guarantees the chosen result.

## Merge commits

Pending diagnostic: what does a merge commit have that an ordinary commit does not? Expected: multiple parents (two for the ordinary two-branch merge). Do not supply this answer before the learner responds.

After diagnosis, define parent links and distinguish a root commit (zero parents), ordinary non-root commit (one), and merge commit (at least two). Display `A->B; C->B; main=A; feature=C; HEAD=main`. Prediction: successful ordinary merge with commit M. Answer: M has parents A and C; main=M; feature=C. Why: both histories become ancestors. Flawed claim: two parents mean two complete directory snapshots in M. Answer: M records one result snapshot and multiple parent links. Narrower question: are a commit's tree and its parent links the same field?

Fallback: show the result snapshot separately from ancestry links. Re-test: ask which old tips remain reachable after deleting feature. Answer: both through M. Edge case: an octopus merge may have more than two parents; a root commit is not a merge merely because it differs from an ordinary one-parent commit.

## Detached HEAD

Tell before application questions: detached HEAD refers directly to a commit. Show `C3->C2->C1; main=C3; HEAD=C2 (direct)`.

Prediction: create C4. Answer: HEAD=C4, parent=C2, main=C3. Why: no current branch reference is attached to HEAD. Flawed claim: committing is impossible here. Answer: commits are possible. Narrower question: can HEAD refer directly to the newly created commit? Connection: how could a new branch keep C4 named? Answer: create a branch at C4.

Fallback: HEAD can name a branch or point directly to a commit; the second case advances HEAD without moving main. Re-test with a new branch created before committing. Edge case: after leaving an unnamed detached tip, a reflog may enable recovery; eventual garbage collection is separate from switching away.

## Practical exercise and assessment

Use a disposable repository only. Teach `git rev-parse HEAD main feature` as printing reference targets, `git symbolic-ref HEAD` as showing the attached branch (it fails when detached), and `git log --graph --oneline --all` as displaying reachable history. Establish the small graph above, ask for predictions, then inspect actual outputs after each switch/commit/merge. Check relationships rather than invented hash values. No commands have been run by the learner yet.

Hold assessment until every Unit 2 skill is at target. Use a fresh graph for each question: predict which branch moves on commit; identify HEAD and files after checkout; decide fast-forward from ancestry; give merge parents; predict detached commit effects. Integrative case: start with two names at one tip, diverge by committing on each, merge, detach at an earlier commit, and create another commit. Require the final named references, parent links, and HEAD target. Independent recall must occur later than explanations; an immediate re-test alone never earns a raise.
# Unit 3 tutor notes — prepared 2026-11-12

Private preparation; no learner exposure or levels implied. Prerequisites: branch references, ancestry, HEAD, fast-forward, merges. Revisit branch movement as spaced review. Sources: [fetch](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-fetch), [pull](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-pull). Assume a normal clone with origin/main mapped to the remote main branch. Explicitly choose pull's integration mode; do not rely on configuration-dependent defaults.

Define origin as a remote nickname; origin/main as a local remote-tracking reference recording a fetched remote state; upstream as a configured tracking relationship. A remote-tracking reference is not a live connection.

Level 3: trace the stated fetch or pull with guidance. Level 4: predict reference and history changes independently. Level 5: explain stale state and divergent-history edge cases clearly. Assess each of the two curriculum concepts separately.

Diagnostic, one question per turn: What does origin/main describe? Can it differ from the server's main? What changes after fetch? What extra work can pull perform? Strong answers explain local state, freshness, and explicit integration; partial familiarity places at 1, accurate definitions at 2, independent application at 4, no idea at 0.

## git.remote-tracking

Show `server main=C3; local main=C1; local origin/main=C1; C3->C2->C1`. Prediction after ordinary fetch: origin/main=C3; local main=C1. Why can local main stay put? Answer: remote-tracking and local branch names serve different purposes. Flawed claim: origin/main always shows the server now. Narrower question: how could the local repository know about a server commit before communicating? New case: the server advances to C4 while offline; local origin/main remains C3. Connection: both main and origin/main are local references, though updated by different usual operations.

Fallback after repeated failures: origin/main records the last fetched state for that mapped branch; fetch updates it without integrating into your local main. Re-test with the server unchanged and an additional local commit. Edge case: the remote rewrites history; a normal configured remote-tracking update can move to a non-descendant. State the refspec assumptions rather than claiming every fetch updates every reference.

## git.fetch-vs-pull

New material: fetch receives objects and updates mapped references. Pull fetches, then integrates into the current branch using the selected mode. Teach `git pull --ff-only` before using it: it permits only a fast-forward integration.

Show the same linear graph as above with HEAD=main. Predict fetch alone versus successful pull --ff-only. Answer: fetch leaves main=C1, pull advances main=C3. Why may fetch be useful before integration? Answer: it lets the user inspect fetched history first. Flawed claim: pull always creates a merge commit. Narrower question: if the fetched tip already descends from main, does moving main require a new commit? Connection: the Unit 2 ancestry rule decides fast-forward.

New case: local main=L2->C1 and server main=R2->C1. Pull --ff-only cannot integrate this divergence; fetched information may still be updated before integration fails. Fallback: separate network transfer from integration. Re-test with linear remote history and a local branch that is already ahead. Edge case: contrast explicitly selected rebase and merge modes on divergence, after defining rebase as replaying local changes onto a new base; require explanation of changed commit identities.

## Practical exercise and assessment

Use disposable local clones and a disposable bare remote; no real remote writes. Before commands, explain fetch origin, pull --ff-only, and rev-parse as operations. Ask the learner to predict and then provide actual reference outputs before and after a fetch and fast-forward pull. Expected relationships are those above; record outputs only when the learner performs the exercise.

Final assessment after both skills reach target: explain a stale origin/main while offline; predict fetch and explicit pull --ff-only effects on a fresh graph; integrative problem with local and remote divergence requires tracking references, identifying why fast-forward fails, and proposing an integration policy. No course completion until the cross-unit assessment covers all earlier concepts too.

reply:
Yes—just reading today, no questions. We’ll leave your levels where they are; reading alone doesn’t earn levels.

A Git branch is a name that points to one commit. That commit links to its parent, which links to its own parent, letting Git trace the history backward.

Suppose you have three commits, with `C` the newest:

```text
A ← B ← C
        ↑
       main
```

The horizontal arrows mean “has this parent.” The branch name `main` points only to `C`. Git reaches `B` and `A` through the links stored in the commits.

Creating another branch, called `experiment`, adds another pointer to the same commit:

```text
A ← B ← C
        ↑
       main
       experiment
```

There’s no need to copy the snapshots or their history. Both names currently identify the same commit.

If you switch to `experiment` and make a new commit, `D`, Git moves that branch’s pointer:

```text
A ← B ← C ← D
        ↑   ↑
       main experiment
```

`D` records the new snapshot and names `C` as its parent. `experiment` now points to `D`; `main` still points to `C`. The existing commits haven’t changed.

That’s why branches are lightweight: creating one gives Git another name to keep track of, and committing on it moves that name forward. The parent links in the commits preserve the path through history.
